title: CI Intermittent segmentation fault in Windows arm64 wheels test (vanilla CPython)
body: I've seen an intermittent segmentation fault in 2 of 13 scheduled Windows arm64 wheel runs so far: once with Python 3.12 and once with Python 3.14. Both logs look similar. The current Python frame is in `sklearn\tree\tests\test_monotonic_tree.py`, line 511, in `test_nd_tree_nodes_values`, while fitting a tree, and Windows reports a fatal access violation.

symptoms_visible: Two of 13 scheduled Windows arm64 wheel runs ended with a Windows fatal access violation.
The failures occurred on vanilla Python 3.12 and Python 3.14, with the current Python frame at line 511 of `test_nd_tree_nodes_values` while fitting a tree.
N0.label: N0 intermittent Windows arm64 access violation reported

symptoms_visible: The isolated test passed for seeds 0 through 99, and repeated local full-suite runs on a Windows ARM laptop did not crash.
The scheduled wheel job still fails intermittently, at roughly one segmentation fault per 15 to 20 runs.
N1.label: N1 seed and local reproduction attempts completed

symptoms_visible: Running the tree test in ten parallel batches repeatedly produces `Access violation - code c0000005`, usually around run 36 to 39.
CDB stops at an ARM64 `ldr` instruction displayed as `_utils_cp314_win_arm64!PyInit__utils+0x70b0`.
N2.label: N2 parallel reproducer found

symptoms_visible: The captured crash dump contains the same `c0000005` access violation and a native stack through the compiled `_utils`, `_criterion`, and `_tree` modules before Python frames.
The native stack has symbol offsets but no source line numbers.
N3.label: N3 native crash stack captured

symptoms_visible: The intermittent access violation remains unexplained, and the Python test shown at the time of the crash may not be the code that corrupted memory.
N3_x.label: N3_x unsupported OpenBLAS attribution and test-skipping rejected

symptoms_visible: I could not trigger the segmentation fault once in roughly 20 runs against the later code and build environment.
The last scheduled segmentation fault I could find was on October 29; the issue has stopped appearing for now.
N_terminal.label: terminal provisionally resolved after sustained non-recurrence

question_patterns: Is the nightly global-random-seed fixture active in this wheel workflow?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I don't think the wheel jobs use the global random seed. My `git grep` only finds it in the unit-test and Azure configurations, not in the wheels workflow.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Yes, every failing wheel job sets the same non-default seed, and the crash is reproducible with that seed.
The wheel job leaves the variable unset, although another unrelated CI workflow sets it.

question_patterns: Can you run the implicated test repeatedly across all supported seed values and report the raw result?
Does `test_nd_tree_nodes_values` reproduce in isolation when tried with seeds 0 through 99?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I ran the isolated test hundreds of times with seed values 0 through 99 on my Windows ARM laptop. The selected cases passed and I could not reproduce the crash.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The isolated test crashes consistently with one particular seed.

question_patterns: Can you leave the seed unset and repeatedly run the full tree package or full scikit-learn test suite on Windows ARM?
Does running a broader test set locally reproduce the intermittent access violation?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I left it running with the full test suite since yesterday on my Windows ARM device, but the segmentation fault did not reproduce locally.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The full suite reproduces the same access violation locally every few runs.

edges.comment: Thread c2-c12. The seed suggestion came from participant2; the reporter checked the workflow configuration and participant1 ran the isolated and full-suite tests. These affected Windows ARM investigation results are folded into one simulated user side.

question_patterns: Can you increase concurrency or system load and repeatedly run the tree tests under a Windows debugger?
Can you find a smaller, more reliable reproducer on Windows ARM and report exactly when it crashes?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I ran ten test batches in parallel, repeated five times. That produces a stable crash around run 36 to 39 with `Access violation - code c0000005`.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Even hundreds of parallel batches complete without an access violation.
The same access violation appears around run 45 instead of run 36 to 39.

question_patterns: What raw location and instruction does the debugger display when the access violation occurs?
Please paste the debugger's exception line and current instruction without interpreting the cause.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: CDB prints `Access violation - code c0000005` and stops at `_utils_cp314_win_arm64!PyInit__utils+0x70b0`, on `ldr d0,[x8,x9]`.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The debugger consistently stops inside an OpenBLAS routine with complete source symbols.

edges.comment: Thread c24-c28. Participant4 found the reliable parallel-batch reproducer on a separate Windows ARM device and supplied the raw CDB location; participant4's setup is explicitly folded into the affected user side.

question_patterns: Can you capture a native CDB backtrace or crash dump when the parallel reproducer fails?
At the debugger prompt, can you run `kb` and paste the resulting native stack?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I captured the dump and ran `kb`. It starts at `_utils_cp314_win_arm64!PyInit__utils+0x70b0`, then includes more `_utils` frames, `_criterion_cp314_win_arm64!PyInit__criterion+0xb1e4`, several `_tree_cp314_win_arm64` offsets, and then Python frames such as `PyObject_Vectorcall` and `PyEval_EvalFrameDefault`.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The native stack identifies a single source line in the test itself and never enters the compiled tree extensions.
The same compiled modules and Python frames appear with slightly different offsets in another dump.

question_patterns: Does the debugger resolve the compiled frames to source files and line numbers?
Was this build compiled with enough debug information to map the native offsets back to generated C or C++ lines?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: No. The dump resolves module and function names or offsets, but it does not show source line numbers for the compiled Cython modules.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Yes, the symbols resolve the first invalid access to an exact generated source line with local variables.

edges.comment: Thread c29-c42. Participant4 captured the dump and reporter pasted its raw stack; participant3 and participant5 noted the lack of debug symbols and line numbers. The stack is evidence only and does not establish which component first corrupted memory.

solution.intent: Treat the intermittent crash as an OpenBLAS or platform-stress limitation and skip the implicated test on Windows ARM.
solution.concrete_example: Assume the crash comes from OpenBLAS under parallel load and skip `test_nd_tree_nodes_values` on Windows ARM so the wheel job can pass.

edges.comment: Thread c32-c34. Participant1 proposed an OpenBLAS explanation and skipping the test; the reporter rejected it because there was insufficient evidence and possible memory corruption could originate before the test visible in the Python stack.

question_patterns: Please rerun the current Windows ARM wheel configuration repeatedly and tell me whether the access violation still occurs.
Can you stress-test today's code and build environment over enough runs to check whether the intermittent failure is still present?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tried it in roughly 20 runs and did not see the segmentation fault a single time. It used to happen much more often, perhaps once every three to five runs.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The current configuration still produces the same access violation every three to five runs.
I completed 25 runs rather than about 20, with no segmentation fault.

solution.intent: Keep the tests enabled and close the issue provisionally after sustained non-recurrence on the current Windows ARM wheel setup, while explicitly leaving the root cause unconfirmed and reopening with stronger instrumentation if it returns.
solution.concrete_example: After about 20 current Windows ARM runs without a crash, close the issue for now rather than skipping coverage. Do not claim a proven cause: the timing could fit the intervening MAE criterion rewrite, but the Cython update is another possibility. If the fault returns, reopen it and use symbolized or AddressSanitizer builds to locate the first invalid memory access.

edges.comment: Thread c47-c55. Participant4 reported that a linked candidate change no longer reproduced the issue, and the reporter independently observed no crash in about 20 current runs and closed provisionally. Participant6 suggested the intervening MAE criterion rewrite as a possible timing explanation; the reporter also identified the Cython update as an alternative. The thread never establishes either hypothesis as the definitive cause.

satisfaction_conditions: Must state that the thread did not establish a definitive root cause; the later MAE criterion rewrite and Cython update are timing-compatible possibilities, not confirmed diagnoses.

Must ground the investigation in the collected evidence: the seed and isolated-test attempts did not reproduce, parallel Windows ARM batches did reproduce `c0000005`, and the native dump showed compiled tree-extension frames without source line numbers.

Must not attribute the crash to OpenBLAS or treat the test visible in the Python stack as proven responsible, because those conclusions were unsupported and the reporter explicitly rejected skipping the test.
Must preserve the Windows ARM test coverage rather than hide the intermittent fault by skipping the test.

Must have the affected side verify sustained non-recurrence over repeated current builds before closing, and must present the closure as provisional with monitoring and reopening if the access violation returns.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced scikit-learn maintainer familiar with CI workflows, pytest configuration, wheel builds, and source searches, but not an expert in Windows native debugging or memory-corruption analysis; other Windows ARM operators are folded into the user side for hardware-specific runs.
persona_hint.communication_style: Collaborative, evidence-driven, and candid about uncertainty; gives concrete logs and commands, challenges unsupported explanations, and prefers preserving test coverage over hiding flakiness.
